topics_covered.title: 1.1 Scope of Macroeconomics, Circular Flow of Income, and Macroeconomic Goals
topics_covered.topic_title: 1.1 Scope of Macroeconomics, Circular Flow of Income, and Macroeconomic Goals
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Four-sector circular flow model (households, firms, government, foreign sector), injections vs leakages.

• National Income Accounting (GDP & GNP): Gross Domestic Product (GDP) measures market value of all final goods/services produced within a nation's borders in a year. Three approaches: 1) Expenditure: GDP = C + I + G + (X - M); 2) Income: Wages + Rent + Interest + Profits + Depreciation + Indirect Taxes; 3) Product/Value-Added (avoids double counting intermediate goods). GNP = GDP + Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA).

• Real vs. Nominal GDP & Inflation: Nominal GDP uses current-year prices; Real GDP uses constant base-year prices. GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100. Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures cost of a fixed basket; Inflation Rate = [(CPI_t - CPI_t-1) / CPI_t-1] × 100. Demand-pull vs. Cost-push inflation.

• Unemployment Types & Business Cycles: Labor Force = Employed + Actively Seeking Unemployed. 1) Frictional (temporary job search/transition); 2) Structural (skills mismatch due to technology); 3) Cyclical (caused by recession/deficient Aggregate Demand). Natural Rate of Unemployment = Frictional + Structural (zero cyclical).

• Macroeconomic Schools & Keynesian Multipliers: Classical (Say's Law, flexible wages/prices, vertical AS, laissez-faire) vs. Keynesian (sticky wages, AD drives output, activist fiscal policy). Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC) + Marginal Propensity to Save (MPS) = 1. Spending Multiplier k = 1 / (1 - MPC) = 1 / MPS. Tax Multiplier = -MPC / (1 - MPC).

• Market Failure, Public Goods & Externalities: Public goods are Non-Rivalrous and Non-Excludable (e.g., national defense, street lighting), leading to the Free-Rider Problem. Negative externalities (pollution: Social Cost > Private Cost → overproduction, corrected by Pigouvian taxes); Positive externalities (vaccination/education: Social Benefit > Private Benefit → underproduction, corrected by subsidies).
key_points: To avoid double counting in GDP, include ONLY final goods and services or sum the Value Added at each production stage.
Since MPC + MPS = 1, if MPC = 0.8, then MPS = 0.2 and the Keynesian Expenditure Multiplier is k = 1 / 0.2 = 5.
Pure public goods possess two defining properties: Non-Rivalry (one person's consumption does not reduce another's) and Non-Excludability.
topics_covered.explanation: Macroeconomics analyzes economy-wide output, inflation, and employment. When private markets fail due to externalities, public goods, or business cycle recessions, targeted fiscal and regulatory policies restore stability.

worked_example.title: Worked Problem: Keynesian Spending Multiplier & GDP Expansion
worked_example.problem: In a closed macroeconomy, the Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC) is 0.75. If the government increases infrastructure expenditure (ΔG) by 20 billion Birr, calculate: (a) Marginal Propensity to Save (MPS), (b) Government Expenditure Multiplier, and (c) Total resulting increase in equilibrium National Income (ΔY).
worked_example.step_solution:
1. Find MPS: Since MPC + MPS = 1, MPS = 1 - 0.75 = 0.25.
2. Calculate Expenditure Multiplier (k): k = 1 / (1 - MPC) = 1 / 0.25 = 4.
3. Calculate Total ΔY: ΔY = k × ΔG = 4 × 20 billion Birr = 80 billion Birr.
worked_example.result: MPS = 0.25, Multiplier k = 4, Total ΔGDP (ΔY) = 80 billion Birr.
worked_example.examiner_note: Note that the Tax Multiplier is always negative and smaller in magnitude by 1: k_tax = -MPC / MPS = -0.75 / 0.25 = -3.

quiz_item.question: If a country's Nominal GDP in 2025 is 600 billion Birr and its GDP Deflator (with base year 2020 = 100) is 120, what is its Real GDP in 2025?
quiz_item.explanation: Real GDP = (Nominal GDP / GDP Deflator) × 100 = (600 billion / 120) × 100 = 5 × 100 = 500 billion Birr.

topics_covered.title: 1.3 Nominal vs. Real GDP, GDP Deflator, CPI, and Business Cycles
topics_covered.topic_title: 1.3 Nominal vs. Real GDP, GDP Deflator, CPI, and Business Cycles
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100, Consumer Price Index inflation rate, expansion, peak, recession, trough.

• Scarcity, Opportunity Cost & PPF: Scarcity is the fundamental economic problem of unlimited wants versus limited resources. Opportunity Cost is the value of the single next-best alternative forgone. Production Possibility Frontier (PPF) illustrates scarcity (points outside are unattainable), efficiency (points on curve), inefficiency (points inside), and increasing opportunity cost (concave bowed-out shape).

• Consumer Behavior (Cardinal vs. Ordinal Utility): Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility: as more units of a good are consumed, Marginal Utility (MU = ΔTU / ΔQ) declines; Total Utility (TU) is maximized when MU = 0. Consumer Equilibrium (Cardinal): MU_X / P_X = MU_Y / P_Y. Ordinal Utility uses Indifference Curves (downward sloping, convex to origin, never intersect; slope = MRS_XY) tangent to the Budget Line (P_X·X + P_Y·Y = Income, slope = -P_X/P_Y).

• Law of Demand, Supply & Equilibrium: Demand (Q_d = a - bP) and Supply (Q_s = c + dP) intersect at Market Equilibrium (Q_d = Q_s). Price changes cause movement ALONG curves; non-price determinants (income, tastes, input costs, technology) SHIFT curves.

• Elasticities of Demand: Price Elasticity of Demand: PED = (%ΔQ_d) / (%ΔP) = (ΔQ / ΔP) × (P / Q). Elastic (|PED| > 1), Inelastic (|PED| < 1), Unitary (|PED| = 1). Cross-Price Elasticity (XED > 0 for substitutes, XED < 0 for complements). Income Elasticity (YED > 0 normal goods, YED < 0 inferior goods).
key_points: Consumer optimum occurs where the Marginal Rate of Substitution equals the price ratio: MRS_XY = MU_X / MU_Y = P_X / P_Y.
When demand is price INELASTIC (|PED| < 1), raising price INCREASES Total Revenue (TR = P × Q); when demand is ELASTIC (|PED| > 1), raising price DECREASES Total Revenue.
Two indifference curves can NEVER intersect because that would violate the transitivity and non-satiation axioms of consumer preference.
topics_covered.explanation: Microeconomic demand and consumer theory explain how rational households allocate limited budgets across goods to maximize utility, and how market prices adjust to clear shortages and surpluses.
topics_covered.detailed_explanation: Microeconomic demand and consumer theory explain how rational households allocate limited budgets across goods to maximize utility, and how market prices adjust to clear shortages and surpluses.
topics_covered.diagram_illustration: Consumer Optimum & Equilibrium: [Indifference Curve Tangent to Budget Line: MRS_XY = P_X/P_Y] ──> [Individual Demand] ──> [Market Equilibrium: Q_d = Q_s].
topics_covered.illustration_analogy: Consumer Optimum & Equilibrium: [Indifference Curve Tangent to Budget Line: MRS_XY = P_X/P_Y] ──> [Individual Demand] ──> [Market Equilibrium: Q_d = Q_s].
topics_covered.ethiopian_context: Agricultural staple crops like teff in Ethiopia exhibit price-inelastic demand, whereas non-essential imported luxury goods exhibit price-elastic demand.
topics_covered.exam_focus: Very high frequency in EUEE: solving market equilibrium equations (Q_d = Q_s), calculating point/arc Price Elasticity of Demand, and finding consumer optimum (MRS_XY = P_X/P_Y).
topics_covered.key_takeaway: Utility is maximized where MU_X/P_X = MU_Y/P_Y; market equilibrium occurs where Q_d = Q_s; |PED| dictates how price changes affect Total Revenue.

worked_example.title: Worked Problem: Market Equilibrium & Price Elasticity of Demand
worked_example.problem: The market for coffee in a regional town is given by the demand function Q_d = 120 - 4P and the supply function Q_s = 20 + 6P, where P is price in Birr and Q is quantity in kg. Find: (a) Equilibrium price and quantity, and (b) Point Price Elasticity of Demand at equilibrium.
worked_example.step_solution:
1. Set Q_d = Q_s for equilibrium: 120 - 4P = 20 + 6P ⟹ 100 = 10P ⟹ P* = 10 Birr.
2. Substitute P* = 10 into Q_d: Q* = 120 - 4(10) = 80 kg.
3. Calculate Point PED: PED = (dQ_d / dP) × (P* / Q*) = (-4) × (10 / 80) = -40 / 80 = -0.5 (or |PED| = 0.5, Inelastic).
worked_example.result: Equilibrium Price P* = 10 Birr, Equilibrium Quantity Q* = 80 kg, |PED| = 0.5 (Price Inelastic).
worked_example.examiner_note: Since |PED| = 0.5 < 1, demand is inelastic at equilibrium, meaning a small price increase will raise total producer revenue.

quiz_item.question: A consumer's Marginal Utility for Good X is 24 utils and for Good Y is 16 utils. If the price of Good X is 6 Birr, what must the price of Good Y be for the consumer to be in utility-maximizing equilibrium?
quiz_item.explanation: Consumer equilibrium requires MU_X / P_X = MU_Y / P_Y. Substituting values: 24 / 6 = 16 / P_Y ⟹ 4 = 16 / P_Y ⟹ P_Y = 16 / 4 = 4 Birr.

book-12-soc-econ_ch_1_topic_topic_1_1__s.detailed_overview: This topic establishes the scope of macroeconomics, differentiating it from microeconomics. The circular flow model demonstrates how income and expenditures circulate within an economy. In a closed economy without government, equilibrium occurs where savings equal investment (S = I). In a full four-sector open economy, total leakages (S + T + M) must equal total injections (I + G + X).

topics_covered.title: Topic 1.1: Scope of Macroeconomics, Circular Flow of Income, and Macroeconomic Goals
short_notes: Macroeconomics studies economy-wide aggregates such as total output, general price levels, and employment.
The four-sector circular flow model comprises households, firms, government, and the foreign sector.
Leakages from the circular flow include savings (S), taxes (T), and imports (M).

worked_examples.title: Calculating Nominal GDP, Real GDP, and GDP Deflator
worked_examples.problem: Suppose an economy produces only wheat. In Year 1 (base year), price is 10 Birr per kg and quantity is 100 kg. In Year 2, price is 15 Birr per kg and quantity is 120 kg. Calculate Nominal GDP, Real GDP, and the GDP Deflator for Year 2.
worked_examples.step_solution:
1. Nominal GDP in Year 2 = P2 × Q2 = 15 Birr × 120 kg = 1,800 Birr.
2. Real GDP in Year 2 (using Base Year 1 prices) = P1 × Q2 = 10 Birr × 120 kg = 1,200 Birr.
3. GDP Deflator in Year 2 = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100 = (1,800 / 1,200) × 100 = 150.
worked_examples.result: Nominal GDP = 1,800 Birr; Real GDP = 1,200 Birr; GDP Deflator = 150.
worked_examples.examiner_note: Always ensure Real GDP uses base-year prices and Nominal GDP uses current-year prices.

worked_examples.title: Calculating the Keynesian Spending Multiplier
worked_examples.problem: Given that the Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC) is 0.75, calculate the value of the spending multiplier and the total change in equilibrium GDP if government spending increases by 200 million Birr.
worked_examples.step_solution:
1. Multiplier k = 1 / (1 - MPC) = 1 / (1 - 0.75) = 1 / 0.25 = 4.
2. Change in GDP = k × Change in Government Spending = 4 × 200 million Birr = 800 million Birr.
worked_examples.result: Multiplier = 4; Total Change in GDP = 800 million Birr.
worked_examples.examiner_note: Remember that MPS = 1 - MPC = 0.25, so k = 1 / 0.25 = 4.

topics_covered.title: Topic 1.2: Measuring GDP and GNP: Product, Income, and Expenditure Approaches
short_notes: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a given period.
Expenditure Approach formula: GDP = C + I + G + (X - M).
Income Approach sums wages, rent, interest, profit, indirect business taxes, and depreciation.
Product/Value-Added Approach sums the value added at each stage of production to prevent double counting intermediate goods.
Gross National Product (GNP) = GDP + Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA).
Net Domestic Product (NDP) = GDP - Depreciation (Capital Consumption Allowance).
Disposable Income (DI) is Personal Income minus personal income taxes.
key_points: Avoid counting intermediate goods to prevent double counting.
NFIA represents income earned by domestic citizens abroad minus income earned by foreigners domestically.
Distinction between GDP (geographic boundary) and GNP (ownership criterion).
topics_covered.explanation: National income accounting provides three equivalent methods to measure economic activity: Expenditure, Income, and Value-Added. The expenditure approach sums consumption, investment, government purchases, and net exports. The value-added approach tracks the incremental value created at each stage of manufacturing or service delivery.

1. Nominal GDP in Year 2 = P2 × Q2 = 15 Birr × 120 kg = 1,800 Birr.
2. Real GDP in Year 2 (using Base Year 1 prices) = P1 × Q2 = 10 Birr × 120 kg = 1,200 Birr.
3. GDP Deflator in Year 2 = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100 = (1,800 / 1,200) × 100 = 150.
worked_examples.result: Nominal GDP = 1,800 Birr; Real GDP = 1,200 Birr; GDP Deflator = 150.
worked_examples.examiner_note: Always ensure Real GDP uses base-year prices and Nominal GDP uses current-year prices.

worked_examples.title: Calculating the Keynesian Spending Multiplier
worked_examples.problem: Given that the Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC) is 0.75, calculate the value of the spending multiplier and the total change in equilibrium GDP if government spending increases by 200 million Birr.
worked_examples.step_solution:
1. Multiplier k = 1 / (1 - MPC) = 1 / (1 - 0.75) = 1 / 0.25 = 4.
2. Change in GDP = k × Change in Government Spending = 4 × 200 million Birr = 800 million Birr.
worked_examples.result: Multiplier = 4; Total Change in GDP = 800 million Birr.
worked_examples.examiner_note: Remember that MPS = 1 - MPC = 0.25, so k = 1 / 0.25 = 4.

book-12-soc-econ_ch_1_topic_scope_of_mac.detailed_overview:
Macroeconomics analyzes economy-wide output, inflation, and employment. When private markets fail due to externalities, public goods, or business cycle recessions, targeted fiscal and regulatory policies restore stability.

Key Takeaway: GDP = C + I + G + (X - M); Real GDP adjusts for inflation; Keynesian Multiplier k = 1 / (1 - MPC); public goods are non-rivalrous and non-excludable.

Ethiopian Context & Real-World Application: Ethiopia's Homegrown Economic Reform (HGER) agenda targets macroeconomic stabilization by curbing inflation, boosting domestic savings, and expanding private-sector investment.

topics_covered.title: 1.1 Scope of Macroeconomics, Circular Flow of Income, and Macroeconomic Goals
topics_covered.topic_title: 1.1 Scope of Macroeconomics, Circular Flow of Income, and Macroeconomic Goals
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Four-sector circular flow model (households, firms, government, foreign sector), injections vs leakages.

• National Income Accounting (GDP & GNP): Gross Domestic Product (GDP) measures market value of all final goods/services produced within a nation's borders in a year. Three approaches: 1) Expenditure: GDP = C + I + G + (X - M); 2) Income: Wages + Rent + Interest + Profits + Depreciation + Indirect Taxes; 3) Product/Value-Added (avoids double counting intermediate goods). GNP = GDP + Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA).

• Real vs. Nominal GDP & Inflation: Nominal GDP uses current-year prices; Real GDP uses constant base-year prices. GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100. Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures cost of a fixed basket; Inflation Rate = [(CPI_t - CPI_t-1) / CPI_t-1] × 100. Demand-pull vs. Cost-push inflation.

• Unemployment Types & Business Cycles: Labor Force = Employed + Actively Seeking Unemployed. 1) Frictional (temporary job search/transition); 2) Structural (skills mismatch due to technology); 3) Cyclical (caused by recession/deficient Aggregate Demand). Natural Rate of Unemployment = Frictional + Structural (zero cyclical).

• Macroeconomic Schools & Keynesian Multipliers: Classical (Say's Law, flexible wages/prices, vertical AS, laissez-faire) vs. Keynesian (sticky wages, AD drives output, activist fiscal policy). Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC) + Marginal Propensity to Save (MPS) = 1. Spending Multiplier k = 1 / (1 - MPC) = 1 / MPS. Tax Multiplier = -MPC / (1 - MPC).

• Market Failure, Public Goods & Externalities: Public goods are Non-Rivalrous and Non-Excludable (e.g., national defense, street lighting), leading to the Free-Rider Problem. Negative externalities (pollution: Social Cost > Private Cost → overproduction, corrected by Pigouvian taxes); Positive externalities (vaccination/education: Social Benefit > Private Benefit → underproduction, corrected by subsidies).
key_points: To avoid double counting in GDP, include ONLY final goods and services or sum the Value Added at each production stage.
Since MPC + MPS = 1, if MPC = 0.8, then MPS = 0.2 and the Keynesian Expenditure Multiplier is k = 1 / 0.2 = 5.
Pure public goods possess two defining properties: Non-Rivalry (one person's consumption does not reduce another's) and Non-Excludability.

worked_examples.title: Worked Problem: Keynesian Spending Multiplier & GDP Expansion
worked_examples.problem: In a closed macroeconomy, the Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC) is 0.75. If the government increases infrastructure expenditure (ΔG) by 20 billion Birr, calculate: (a) Marginal Propensity to Save (MPS), (b) Government Expenditure Multiplier, and (c) Total resulting increase in equilibrium National Income (ΔY).
worked_examples.step_solution:
1. Find MPS: Since MPC + MPS = 1, MPS = 1 - 0.75 = 0.25.
2. Calculate Expenditure Multiplier (k): k = 1 / (1 - MPC) = 1 / 0.25 = 4.
3. Calculate Total ΔY: ΔY = k × ΔG = 4 × 20 billion Birr = 80 billion Birr.
worked_examples.result: MPS = 0.25, Multiplier k = 4, Total ΔGDP (ΔY) = 80 billion Birr.
worked_examples.examiner_note: Note that the Tax Multiplier is always negative and smaller in magnitude by 1: k_tax = -MPC / MPS = -0.75 / 0.25 = -3.

practice_quiz.question: If a country's Nominal GDP in 2025 is 600 billion Birr and its GDP Deflator (with base year 2020 = 100) is 120, what is its Real GDP in 2025?
practice_quiz.explanation: Real GDP = (Nominal GDP / GDP Deflator) × 100 = (600 billion / 120) × 100 = 5 × 100 = 500 billion Birr.

book-12-soc-econ_ch_1_Scope of Macroecon.detailed_overview:
Macroeconomics analyzes economy-wide output, inflation, and employment. When private markets fail due to externalities, public goods, or business cycle recessions, targeted fiscal and regulatory policies restore stability.

Key Takeaway: GDP = C + I + G + (X - M); Real GDP adjusts for inflation; Keynesian Multiplier k = 1 / (1 - MPC); public goods are non-rivalrous and non-excludable.

Ethiopian Context & Real-World Application: Ethiopia's Homegrown Economic Reform (HGER) agenda targets macroeconomic stabilization by curbing inflation, boosting domestic savings, and expanding private-sector investment.

topics_covered.title: 1.1 Scope of Macroeconomics, Circular Flow of Income, and Macroeconomic Goals
topics_covered.topic_title: 1.1 Scope of Macroeconomics, Circular Flow of Income, and Macroeconomic Goals
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Four-sector circular flow model (households, firms, government, foreign sector), injections vs leakages.

• National Income Accounting (GDP & GNP): Gross Domestic Product (GDP) measures market value of all final goods/services produced within a nation's borders in a year. Three approaches: 1) Expenditure: GDP = C + I + G + (X - M); 2) Income: Wages + Rent + Interest + Profits + Depreciation + Indirect Taxes; 3) Product/Value-Added (avoids double counting intermediate goods). GNP = GDP + Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA).

• Real vs. Nominal GDP & Inflation: Nominal GDP uses current-year prices; Real GDP uses constant base-year prices. GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100. Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures cost of a fixed basket; Inflation Rate = [(CPI_t - CPI_t-1) / CPI_t-1] × 100. Demand-pull vs. Cost-push inflation.

• Unemployment Types & Business Cycles: Labor Force = Employed + Actively Seeking Unemployed. 1) Frictional (temporary job search/transition); 2) Structural (skills mismatch due to technology); 3) Cyclical (caused by recession/deficient Aggregate Demand). Natural Rate of Unemployment = Frictional + Structural (zero cyclical).

• Macroeconomic Schools & Keynesian Multipliers: Classical (Say's Law, flexible wages/prices, vertical AS, laissez-faire) vs. Keynesian (sticky wages, AD drives output, activist fiscal policy). Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC) + Marginal Propensity to Save (MPS) = 1. Spending Multiplier k = 1 / (1 - MPC) = 1 / MPS. Tax Multiplier = -MPC / (1 - MPC).

• Market Failure, Public Goods & Externalities: Public goods are Non-Rivalrous and Non-Excludable (e.g., national defense, street lighting), leading to the Free-Rider Problem. Negative externalities (pollution: Social Cost > Private Cost → overproduction, corrected by Pigouvian taxes); Positive externalities (vaccination/education: Social Benefit > Private Benefit → underproduction, corrected by subsidies).
key_points: To avoid double counting in GDP, include ONLY final goods and services or sum the Value Added at each production stage.
Since MPC + MPS = 1, if MPC = 0.8, then MPS = 0.2 and the Keynesian Expenditure Multiplier is k = 1 / 0.2 = 5.
Pure public goods possess two defining properties: Non-Rivalry (one person's consumption does not reduce another's) and Non-Excludability.

worked_examples.title: Worked Problem: Keynesian Spending Multiplier & GDP Expansion
worked_examples.problem: In a closed macroeconomy, the Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC) is 0.75. If the government increases infrastructure expenditure (ΔG) by 20 billion Birr, calculate: (a) Marginal Propensity to Save (MPS), (b) Government Expenditure Multiplier, and (c) Total resulting increase in equilibrium National Income (ΔY).
worked_examples.step_solution:
1. Find MPS: Since MPC + MPS = 1, MPS = 1 - 0.75 = 0.25.
2. Calculate Expenditure Multiplier (k): k = 1 / (1 - MPC) = 1 / 0.25 = 4.
3. Calculate Total ΔY: ΔY = k × ΔG = 4 × 20 billion Birr = 80 billion Birr.
worked_examples.result: MPS = 0.25, Multiplier k = 4, Total ΔGDP (ΔY) = 80 billion Birr.
worked_examples.examiner_note: Note that the Tax Multiplier is always negative and smaller in magnitude by 1: k_tax = -MPC / MPS = -0.75 / 0.25 = -3.

### 1. Theoretical Foundations & Governing Principles
Macroeconomics analyzes economy-wide output, inflation, and employment. When private markets fail due to externalities, public goods, or business cycle recessions, targeted fiscal and regulatory policies restore stability.

**Curriculum Syllabus Alignment:** Four-sector circular flow model (households, firms, government, foreign sector), injections vs leakages.

### 2. Systematic Concept Breakdown & Mechanisms
- **Key Principle**: To avoid double counting in GDP, include ONLY final goods and services or sum the Value Added at each production stage.
- **Key Principle**: Since MPC + MPS = 1, if MPC = 0.8, then MPS = 0.2 and the Keynesian Expenditure Multiplier is k = 1 / 0.2 = 5.
- **Pure public goods possess two defining properties**: Pure public goods possess two defining properties: Non-Rivalry (one person's consumption does not reduce another's) and Non-Excludability.

### 3. Core Reference Table & Visual Schema
**Visual / Experimental Schema:**
```text
Keynesian Multiplier Chain: [ΔGovernment Spending ΔG = 100M] ──(MPC = 0.8)──> [Multiplier k = 1/(1-0.8) = 5] ──> [Total ΔGDP = 5 × 100M = 500M Birr].
```

short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Four-sector circular flow model (households, firms, government, foreign sector), injections vs leakages.

• National Income Accounting (GDP & GNP): Gross Domestic Product (GDP) measures market value of all final goods/services produced within a nation's borders in a year. Negative externalities (pollution: Social Cost > Private Cost → overproduction, corrected by Pigouvian taxes); Positive externalities (vaccination/education: Social Benefit > Private Benefit → underproduction, corrected by subsidies).

worked_examples.title: Worked Problem: Keynesian Spending Multiplier & GDP Expansion
worked_examples.problem: In a closed macroeconomy, the Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC) is 0.75. If the government increases infrastructure expenditure (ΔG) by 20 billion Birr, calculate: (a) Marginal Propensity to Save (MPS), (b) Government Expenditure Multiplier, and (c) Total resulting increase in equilibrium National Income (ΔY).
worked_examples.step_solution:
1. Find MPS: Since MPC + MPS = 1, MPS = 1 - 0.75 = 0.25.
2. Calculate Expenditure Multiplier (k): k = 1 / (1 - MPC) = 1 / 0.25 = 4.
3. Calculate Total ΔY: ΔY = k × ΔG = 4 × 20 billion Birr = 80 billion Birr.
worked_examples.result: MPS = 0.25, Multiplier k = 4, Total ΔGDP (ΔY) = 80 billion Birr.
worked_examples.examiner_note: Note that the Tax Multiplier is always negative and smaller in magnitude by 1: k_tax = -MPC / MPS = -0.75 / 0.25 = -3.

- **1.1 Scope of Macroeconomics, Circular Flow of Income, and Macroeconomic Goals**: Ethiopia's Homegrown Economic Reform (HGER) agenda targets macroeconomic stabilization by curbing inflation, boosting domestic savings, and expanding private-sector investment.

- **1.3 Nominal vs. Real GDP, GDP Deflator, CPI, and Business Cycles**: Agricultural staple crops like teff in Ethiopia exhibit price-inelastic demand, whereas non-essential imported luxury goods exhibit price-elastic demand.

- **1.1 Scope of Macroeconomics, Circular Flow of Income, and Macroeconomic Goals**: Universal EUEE questions: calculating GDP via expenditure method, computing Real GDP and GDP Deflator, applying the Keynesian spending multiplier k = 1/(1-MPC), and classifying unemployment types.

worked_example.title: Worked Problem: Keynesian Spending Multiplier & GDP Expansion
worked_example.problem: In a closed macroeconomy, the Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC) is 0.75. If the government increases infrastructure expenditure (ΔG) by 20 billion Birr, calculate: (a) Marginal Propensity to Save (MPS), (b) Government Expenditure Multiplier, and (c) Total resulting increase in equilibrium National Income (ΔY).
worked_example.step_solution:
1. Find MPS: Since MPC + MPS = 1, MPS = 1 - 0.75 = 0.25.
2. Calculate Expenditure Multiplier (k): k = 1 / (1 - MPC) = 1 / 0.25 = 4.
3. Calculate Total ΔY: ΔY = k × ΔG = 4 × 20 billion Birr = 80 billion Birr.
worked_example.result: MPS = 0.25, Multiplier k = 4, Total ΔGDP (ΔY) = 80 billion Birr.
worked_example.examiner_note: Note that the Tax Multiplier is always negative and smaller in magnitude by 1: k_tax = -MPC / MPS = -0.75 / 0.25 = -3.

quiz_item.question: If a country's Nominal GDP in 2025 is 600 billion Birr and its GDP Deflator (with base year 2020 = 100) is 120, what is its Real GDP in 2025?
quiz_item.explanation: Real GDP = (Nominal GDP / GDP Deflator) × 100 = (600 billion / 120) × 100 = 5 × 100 = 500 billion Birr.

topics_covered.title: 1.2 Measuring GDP and GNP: Product, Income, and Expenditure Approaches
topics_covered.topic_title: 1.2 Measuring GDP and GNP: Product, Income, and Expenditure Approaches
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: GDP = C + I + G + (X - M), Value-Added method avoiding double counting, GNP = GDP + NFIA, NDP, NI, PI, and DI.

• National Income Accounting (GDP & GNP): Gross Domestic Product (GDP) measures market value of all final goods/services produced within a nation's borders in a year. Three approaches: 1) Expenditure: GDP = C + I + G + (X - M); 2) Income: Wages + Rent + Interest + Profits + Depreciation + Indirect Taxes; 3) Product/Value-Added (avoids double counting intermediate goods). GNP = GDP + Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA).

• Real vs. Nominal GDP & Inflation: Nominal GDP uses current-year prices; Real GDP uses constant base-year prices. GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100. Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures cost of a fixed basket; Inflation Rate = [(CPI_t - CPI_t-1) / CPI_t-1] × 100. Demand-pull vs. Cost-push inflation.

• Unemployment Types & Business Cycles: Labor Force = Employed + Actively Seeking Unemployed. 1) Frictional (temporary job search/transition); 2) Structural (skills mismatch due to technology); 3) Cyclical (caused by recession/deficient Aggregate Demand). Natural Rate of Unemployment = Frictional + Structural (zero cyclical).

• Macroeconomic Schools & Keynesian Multipliers: Classical (Say's Law, flexible wages/prices, vertical AS, laissez-faire) vs. Keynesian (sticky wages, AD drives output, activist fiscal policy). Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC) + Marginal Propensity to Save (MPS) = 1. Spending Multiplier k = 1 / (1 - MPC) = 1 / MPS. Tax Multiplier = -MPC / (1 - MPC).

• Market Failure, Public Goods & Externalities: Public goods are Non-Rivalrous and Non-Excludable (e.g., national defense, street lighting), leading to the Free-Rider Problem. Negative externalities (pollution: Social Cost > Private Cost → overproduction, corrected by Pigouvian taxes); Positive externalities (vaccination/education: Social Benefit > Private Benefit → underproduction, corrected by subsidies).
key_points: To avoid double counting in GDP, include ONLY final goods and services or sum the Value Added at each production stage.
Since MPC + MPS = 1, if MPC = 0.8, then MPS = 0.2 and the Keynesian Expenditure Multiplier is k = 1 / 0.2 = 5.
Pure public goods possess two defining properties: Non-Rivalry (one person's consumption does not reduce another's) and Non-Excludability.

topics_covered.title: 1.3 Nominal vs. Real GDP, GDP Deflator, CPI, and Business Cycles
topics_covered.topic_title: 1.3 Nominal vs. Real GDP, GDP Deflator, CPI, and Business Cycles
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100, Consumer Price Index inflation rate, expansion, peak, recession, trough.

• Scarcity, Opportunity Cost & PPF: Scarcity is the fundamental economic problem of unlimited wants versus limited resources. Opportunity Cost is the value of the single next-best alternative forgone. Production Possibility Frontier (PPF) illustrates scarcity (points outside are unattainable), efficiency (points on curve), inefficiency (points inside), and increasing opportunity cost (concave bowed-out shape).

• Consumer Behavior (Cardinal vs. Ordinal Utility): Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility: as more units of a good are consumed, Marginal Utility (MU = ΔTU / ΔQ) declines; Total Utility (TU) is maximized when MU = 0. Consumer Equilibrium (Cardinal): MU_X / P_X = MU_Y / P_Y. Ordinal Utility uses Indifference Curves (downward sloping, convex to origin, never intersect; slope = MRS_XY) tangent to the Budget Line (P_X·X + P_Y·Y = Income, slope = -P_X/P_Y).

• Law of Demand, Supply & Equilibrium: Demand (Q_d = a - bP) and Supply (Q_s = c + dP) intersect at Market Equilibrium (Q_d = Q_s). Price changes cause movement ALONG curves; non-price determinants (income, tastes, input costs, technology) SHIFT curves.

• Elasticities of Demand: Price Elasticity of Demand: PED = (%ΔQ_d) / (%ΔP) = (ΔQ / ΔP) × (P / Q). Elastic (|PED| > 1), Inelastic (|PED| < 1), Unitary (|PED| = 1). Cross-Price Elasticity (XED > 0 for substitutes, XED < 0 for complements). Income Elasticity (YED > 0 normal goods, YED < 0 inferior goods).
key_points: Consumer optimum occurs where the Marginal Rate of Substitution equals the price ratio: MRS_XY = MU_X / MU_Y = P_X / P_Y.
When demand is price INELASTIC (|PED| < 1), raising price INCREASES Total Revenue (TR = P × Q); when demand is ELASTIC (|PED| > 1), raising price DECREASES Total Revenue.
Two indifference curves can NEVER intersect because that would violate the transitivity and non-satiation axioms of consumer preference.

### 1. Theoretical Foundations & Governing Principles
Microeconomic demand and consumer theory explain how rational households allocate limited budgets across goods to maximize utility, and how market prices adjust to clear shortages and surpluses.

**Curriculum Syllabus Alignment:** GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100, Consumer Price Index inflation rate, expansion, peak, recession, trough.

### 2. Systematic Concept Breakdown & Mechanisms
- **Consumer optimum occurs where the Marginal Rate of Substitution equals the price ratio**: Consumer optimum occurs where the Marginal Rate of Substitution equals the price ratio: MRS_XY = MU_X / MU_Y = P_X / P_Y.
- **Key Principle**: When demand is price INELASTIC (|PED| < 1), raising price INCREASES Total Revenue (TR = P × Q); when demand is ELASTIC (|PED| > 1), raising price DECREASES Total Revenue.
- **Key Principle**: Two indifference curves can NEVER intersect because that would violate the transitivity and non-satiation axioms of consumer preference.

**Visual / Experimental Schema:**
```text
Consumer Optimum & Equilibrium: [Indifference Curve Tangent to Budget Line: MRS_XY = P_X/P_Y] ──> [Individual Demand] ──> [Market Equilibrium: Q_d = Q_s].
```

worked_example.title: Worked Problem: Market Equilibrium & Price Elasticity of Demand
worked_example.problem: The market for coffee in a regional town is given by the demand function Q_d = 120 - 4P and the supply function Q_s = 20 + 6P, where P is price in Birr and Q is quantity in kg. Find: (a) Equilibrium price and quantity, and (b) Point Price Elasticity of Demand at equilibrium.
worked_example.step_solution:
1. Set Q_d = Q_s for equilibrium: 120 - 4P = 20 + 6P ⟹ 100 = 10P ⟹ P* = 10 Birr.
2. Substitute P* = 10 into Q_d: Q* = 120 - 4(10) = 80 kg.
3. Calculate Point PED: PED = (dQ_d / dP) × (P* / Q*) = (-4) × (10 / 80) = -40 / 80 = -0.5 (or |PED| = 0.5, Inelastic).
worked_example.result: Equilibrium Price P* = 10 Birr, Equilibrium Quantity Q* = 80 kg, |PED| = 0.5 (Price Inelastic).
worked_example.examiner_note: Since |PED| = 0.5 < 1, demand is inelastic at equilibrium, meaning a small price increase will raise total producer revenue.

quiz_item.question: A consumer's Marginal Utility for Good X is 24 utils and for Good Y is 16 utils. If the price of Good X is 6 Birr, what must the price of Good Y be for the consumer to be in utility-maximizing equilibrium?
quiz_item.explanation: Consumer equilibrium requires MU_X / P_X = MU_Y / P_Y. Substituting values: 24 / 6 = 16 / P_Y ⟹ 4 = 16 / P_Y ⟹ P_Y = 16 / 4 = 4 Birr.

worked_examples.title: Worked Problem: Market Equilibrium & Price Elasticity of Demand (1.3 Nominal vs. Real GDP, GDP Deflator, CPI, and Business Cycles)
worked_examples.problem: The market for coffee in a regional town is given by the demand function Q_d = 120 - 4P and the supply function Q_s = 20 + 6P, where P is price in Birr and Q is quantity in kg. Find: (a) Equilibrium price and quantity, and (b) Point Price Elasticity of Demand at equilibrium.
worked_examples.step_solution:
1. Set Q_d = Q_s for equilibrium: 120 - 4P = 20 + 6P ⟹ 100 = 10P ⟹ P* = 10 Birr.
2. Substitute P* = 10 into Q_d: Q* = 120 - 4(10) = 80 kg.
3. Calculate Point PED: PED = (dQ_d / dP) × (P* / Q*) = (-4) × (10 / 80) = -40 / 80 = -0.5 (or |PED| = 0.5, Inelastic).
worked_examples.result: Equilibrium Price P* = 10 Birr, Equilibrium Quantity Q* = 80 kg, |PED| = 0.5 (Price Inelastic).
worked_examples.examiner_note: Since |PED| = 0.5 < 1, demand is inelastic at equilibrium, meaning a small price increase will raise total producer revenue.

quick_example.problem: In a closed macroeconomy, the Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC) is 0.75. If the government increases infrastructure expenditure (ΔG) by 20 billion Birr, calculate: (a) Marginal Propensity to Save (MPS), (b) Government Expenditure Multiplier, and (c) Total resulting increase in equilibrium National Income (ΔY).
quick_example.step_solution:
1. Find MPS: Since MPC + MPS = 1, MPS = 1 - 0.75 = 0.25.
2. Calculate Expenditure Multiplier (k): k = 1 / (1 - MPC) = 1 / 0.25 = 4.
3. Calculate Total ΔY: ΔY = k × ΔG = 4 × 20 billion Birr = 80 billion Birr.
quick_example.result: MPS = 0.25, Multiplier k = 4, Total ΔGDP (ΔY) = 80 billion Birr.

practice_quiz.explanation: Real GDP = (Nominal GDP / GDP Deflator) × 100 = (600 billion / 120) × 100 = 5 × 100 = 500 billion Birr.

topics_covered.topic_title: 1.2 Measuring GDP and GNP: Product, Income, and Expenditure Approaches
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: GDP = C + I + G + (X - M), Value-Added method avoiding double counting, GNP = GDP + NFIA, NDP, NI, PI, and DI.

• National Income Accounting (GDP & GNP): Gross Domestic Product (GDP) measures market value of all final goods/services produced within a nation's borders in a year. Three approaches: 1) Expenditure: GDP = C + I + G + (X - M); 2) Income: Wages + Rent + Interest + Profits + Depreciation + Indirect Taxes; 3) Product/Value-Added (avoids double counting intermediate goods). GNP = GDP + Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA).

• Real vs. Nominal GDP & Inflation: Nominal GDP uses current-year prices; Real GDP uses constant base-year prices. GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100. Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures cost of a fixed basket; Inflation Rate = [(CPI_t - CPI_t-1) / CPI_t-1] × 100. Demand-pull vs. Cost-push inflation.

• Unemployment Types & Business Cycles: Labor Force = Employed + Actively Seeking Unemployed. 1) Frictional (temporary job search/transition); 2) Structural (skills mismatch due to technology); 3) Cyclical (caused by recession/deficient Aggregate Demand). Natural Rate of Unemployment = Frictional + Structural (zero cyclical).

• Macroeconomic Schools & Keynesian Multipliers: Classical (Say's Law, flexible wages/prices, vertical AS, laissez-faire) vs. Keynesian (sticky wages, AD drives output, activist fiscal policy). Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC) + Marginal Propensity to Save (MPS) = 1. Spending Multiplier k = 1 / (1 - MPC) = 1 / MPS. Tax Multiplier = -MPC / (1 - MPC).

• Market Failure, Public Goods & Externalities: Public goods are Non-Rivalrous and Non-Excludable (e.g., national defense, street lighting), leading to the Free-Rider Problem. Negative externalities (pollution: Social Cost > Private Cost → overproduction, corrected by Pigouvian taxes); Positive externalities (vaccination/education: Social Benefit > Private Benefit → underproduction, corrected by subsidies).
key_points: To avoid double counting in GDP, include ONLY final goods and services or sum the Value Added at each production stage.
Since MPC + MPS = 1, if MPC = 0.8, then MPS = 0.2 and the Keynesian Expenditure Multiplier is k = 1 / 0.2 = 5.
Pure public goods possess two defining properties: Non-Rivalry (one person's consumption does not reduce another's) and Non-Excludability.

core_formulas_rules.units_conditions: Standard Ethiopian curriculum specifications and SI units apply.

core_formulas_rules.explanation: National Income Accounting (GDP & GNP): Gross Domestic Product (GDP) measures market value of all final goods/services produced within a nation's borders in a year. Three approaches: 1) Expenditure: GDP = C + I + G + (X - M); 2) Income: Wages + Rent + Interest + Profits + Depreciation + Indirect Taxes; 3) Product/Value-Added (avoids double counting intermediate goods). GNP = GDP + Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA).
core_formulas_rules.units_conditions: Standard Ethiopian curriculum specifications and SI units apply.

core_formulas_rules.explanation: Real vs. Nominal GDP & Inflation: Nominal GDP uses current-year prices; Real GDP uses constant base-year prices. GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100. Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures cost of a fixed basket; Inflation Rate = [(CPI_t - CPI_t-1) / CPI_t-1] × 100. Demand-pull vs. Cost-push inflation.
core_formulas_rules.units_conditions: Standard Ethiopian curriculum specifications and SI units apply.

core_formulas_rules.explanation: Unemployment Types & Business Cycles: Labor Force = Employed + Actively Seeking Unemployed. 1) Frictional (temporary job search/transition); 2) Structural (skills mismatch due to technology); 3) Cyclical (caused by recession/deficient Aggregate Demand). Natural Rate of Unemployment = Frictional + Structural (zero cyclical).
core_formulas_rules.units_conditions: Standard Ethiopian curriculum specifications and SI units apply.

core_formulas_rules.explanation: Macroeconomic Schools & Keynesian Multipliers: Classical (Say's Law, flexible wages/prices, vertical AS, laissez-faire) vs. Keynesian (sticky wages, AD drives output, activist fiscal policy). Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC) + Marginal Propensity to Save (MPS) = 1. Spending Multiplier k = 1 / (1 - MPC) = 1 / MPS. Tax Multiplier = -MPC / (1 - MPC).
core_formulas_rules.units_conditions: Standard Ethiopian curriculum specifications and SI units apply.

core_formulas_rules.explanation: Market Failure, Public Goods & Externalities: Public goods are Non-Rivalrous and Non-Excludable (e.g., national defense, street lighting), leading to the Free-Rider Problem. Negative externalities (pollution: Social Cost > Private Cost → overproduction, corrected by Pigouvian taxes); Positive externalities (vaccination/education: Social Benefit > Private Benefit → underproduction, corrected by subsidies).
core_formulas_rules.units_conditions: Standard Ethiopian curriculum specifications and SI units apply.

worked_examples.title: Worked Problem: Keynesian Spending Multiplier & GDP Expansion
worked_examples.problem: In a closed macroeconomy, the Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC) is 0.75. If the government increases infrastructure expenditure (ΔG) by 20 billion Birr, calculate: (a) Marginal Propensity to Save (MPS), (b) Government Expenditure Multiplier, and (c) Total resulting increase in equilibrium National Income (ΔY).
worked_examples.step_solution:
1. Find MPS: Since MPC + MPS = 1, MPS = 1 - 0.75 = 0.25.
2. Calculate Expenditure Multiplier (k): k = 1 / (1 - MPC) = 1 / 0.25 = 4.
3. Calculate Total ΔY: ΔY = k × ΔG = 4 × 20 billion Birr = 80 billion Birr.
worked_examples.result: MPS = 0.25, Multiplier k = 4, Total ΔGDP (ΔY) = 80 billion Birr.
worked_examples.examiner_note: Note that the Tax Multiplier is always negative and smaller in magnitude by 1: k_tax = -MPC / MPS = -0.75 / 0.25 = -3.

practice_quiz.question: If a country's Nominal GDP in 2025 is 600 billion Birr and its GDP Deflator (with base year 2020 = 100) is 120, what is its Real GDP in 2025?

book-12-soc-econ_ch_1_topic_nominal_vs__.detailed_overview:
Microeconomic demand and consumer theory explain how rational households allocate limited budgets across goods to maximize utility, and how market prices adjust to clear shortages and surpluses.

Key Takeaway: Utility is maximized where MU_X/P_X = MU_Y/P_Y; market equilibrium occurs where Q_d = Q_s; |PED| dictates how price changes affect Total Revenue.

Ethiopian Context & Real-World Application: Agricultural staple crops like teff in Ethiopia exhibit price-inelastic demand, whereas non-essential imported luxury goods exhibit price-elastic demand.

topics_covered.title: 1.3 Nominal vs. Real GDP, GDP Deflator, CPI, and Business Cycles
topics_covered.topic_title: 1.3 Nominal vs. Real GDP, GDP Deflator, CPI, and Business Cycles
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100, Consumer Price Index inflation rate, expansion, peak, recession, trough.

• Scarcity, Opportunity Cost & PPF: Scarcity is the fundamental economic problem of unlimited wants versus limited resources. Opportunity Cost is the value of the single next-best alternative forgone. Production Possibility Frontier (PPF) illustrates scarcity (points outside are unattainable), efficiency (points on curve), inefficiency (points inside), and increasing opportunity cost (concave bowed-out shape).

• Consumer Behavior (Cardinal vs. Ordinal Utility): Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility: as more units of a good are consumed, Marginal Utility (MU = ΔTU / ΔQ) declines; Total Utility (TU) is maximized when MU = 0. Consumer Equilibrium (Cardinal): MU_X / P_X = MU_Y / P_Y. Ordinal Utility uses Indifference Curves (downward sloping, convex to origin, never intersect; slope = MRS_XY) tangent to the Budget Line (P_X·X + P_Y·Y = Income, slope = -P_X/P_Y).

• Law of Demand, Supply & Equilibrium: Demand (Q_d = a - bP) and Supply (Q_s = c + dP) intersect at Market Equilibrium (Q_d = Q_s). Price changes cause movement ALONG curves; non-price determinants (income, tastes, input costs, technology) SHIFT curves.

• Elasticities of Demand: Price Elasticity of Demand: PED = (%ΔQ_d) / (%ΔP) = (ΔQ / ΔP) × (P / Q). Elastic (|PED| > 1), Inelastic (|PED| < 1), Unitary (|PED| = 1). Cross-Price Elasticity (XED > 0 for substitutes, XED < 0 for complements). Income Elasticity (YED > 0 normal goods, YED < 0 inferior goods).
key_points: Consumer optimum occurs where the Marginal Rate of Substitution equals the price ratio: MRS_XY = MU_X / MU_Y = P_X / P_Y.
When demand is price INELASTIC (|PED| < 1), raising price INCREASES Total Revenue (TR = P × Q); when demand is ELASTIC (|PED| > 1), raising price DECREASES Total Revenue.
Two indifference curves can NEVER intersect because that would violate the transitivity and non-satiation axioms of consumer preference.

worked_examples.title: Worked Problem: Market Equilibrium & Price Elasticity of Demand
worked_examples.problem: The market for coffee in a regional town is given by the demand function Q_d = 120 - 4P and the supply function Q_s = 20 + 6P, where P is price in Birr and Q is quantity in kg. Find: (a) Equilibrium price and quantity, and (b) Point Price Elasticity of Demand at equilibrium.
worked_examples.step_solution:
1. Set Q_d = Q_s for equilibrium: 120 - 4P = 20 + 6P ⟹ 100 = 10P ⟹ P* = 10 Birr.
2. Substitute P* = 10 into Q_d: Q* = 120 - 4(10) = 80 kg.
3. Calculate Point PED: PED = (dQ_d / dP) × (P* / Q*) = (-4) × (10 / 80) = -40 / 80 = -0.5 (or |PED| = 0.5, Inelastic).
worked_examples.result: Equilibrium Price P* = 10 Birr, Equilibrium Quantity Q* = 80 kg, |PED| = 0.5 (Price Inelastic).
worked_examples.examiner_note: Since |PED| = 0.5 < 1, demand is inelastic at equilibrium, meaning a small price increase will raise total producer revenue.

quick_example.problem: The market for coffee in a regional town is given by the demand function Q_d = 120 - 4P and the supply function Q_s = 20 + 6P, where P is price in Birr and Q is quantity in kg. Find: (a) Equilibrium price and quantity, and (b) Point Price Elasticity of Demand at equilibrium.
quick_example.step_solution:
1. Set Q_d = Q_s for equilibrium: 120 - 4P = 20 + 6P ⟹ 100 = 10P ⟹ P* = 10 Birr.
2. Substitute P* = 10 into Q_d: Q* = 120 - 4(10) = 80 kg.
3. Calculate Point PED: PED = (dQ_d / dP) × (P* / Q*) = (-4) × (10 / 80) = -40 / 80 = -0.5 (or |PED| = 0.5, Inelastic).
quick_example.result: Equilibrium Price P* = 10 Birr, Equilibrium Quantity Q* = 80 kg, |PED| = 0.5 (Price Inelastic).

practice_quiz.question: A consumer's Marginal Utility for Good X is 24 utils and for Good Y is 16 utils. If the price of Good X is 6 Birr, what must the price of Good Y be for the consumer to be in utility-maximizing equilibrium?
practice_quiz.explanation: Consumer equilibrium requires MU_X / P_X = MU_Y / P_Y. Substituting values: 24 / 6 = 16 / P_Y ⟹ 4 = 16 / P_Y ⟹ P_Y = 16 / 4 = 4 Birr.

worked_examples.title: Worked Problem: Market Equilibrium & Price Elasticity of Demand
worked_examples.problem: The market for coffee in a regional town is given by the demand function Q_d = 120 - 4P and the supply function Q_s = 20 + 6P, where P is price in Birr and Q is quantity in kg. Find: (a) Equilibrium price and quantity, and (b) Point Price Elasticity of Demand at equilibrium.
worked_examples.step_solution:
1. Set Q_d = Q_s for equilibrium: 120 - 4P = 20 + 6P ⟹ 100 = 10P ⟹ P* = 10 Birr.
2. Substitute P* = 10 into Q_d: Q* = 120 - 4(10) = 80 kg.
3. Calculate Point PED: PED = (dQ_d / dP) × (P* / Q*) = (-4) × (10 / 80) = -40 / 80 = -0.5 (or |PED| = 0.5, Inelastic).
worked_examples.result: Equilibrium Price P* = 10 Birr, Equilibrium Quantity Q* = 80 kg, |PED| = 0.5 (Price Inelastic).
worked_examples.examiner_note: Since |PED| = 0.5 < 1, demand is inelastic at equilibrium, meaning a small price increase will raise total producer revenue.

practice_quiz.question: A consumer's Marginal Utility for Good X is 24 utils and for Good Y is 16 utils. If the price of Good X is 6 Birr, what must the price of Good Y be for the consumer to be in utility-maximizing equilibrium?

### 1. Theoretical Foundations & Governing Principles
Microeconomic demand and consumer theory explain how rational households allocate limited budgets across goods to maximize utility, and how market prices adjust to clear shortages and surpluses.

**Curriculum Syllabus Alignment:** GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100, Consumer Price Index inflation rate, expansion, peak, recession, trough.

### 2. Systematic Concept Breakdown & Mechanisms
- **Consumer optimum occurs where the Marginal Rate of Substitution equals the price ratio**: Consumer optimum occurs where the Marginal Rate of Substitution equals the price ratio: MRS_XY = MU_X / MU_Y = P_X / P_Y.
- **Key Principle**: When demand is price INELASTIC (|PED| < 1), raising price INCREASES Total Revenue (TR = P × Q); when demand is ELASTIC (|PED| > 1), raising price DECREASES Total Revenue.
- **Key Principle**: Two indifference curves can NEVER intersect because that would violate the transitivity and non-satiation axioms of consumer preference.

### 3. Core Reference Table & Visual Schema
**Visual / Experimental Schema:**
```text
Consumer Optimum & Equilibrium: [Indifference Curve Tangent to Budget Line: MRS_XY = P_X/P_Y] ──> [Individual Demand] ──> [Market Equilibrium: Q_d = Q_s].
```

| **Examination Traps** | Very high frequency in EUEE: solving market equilibrium equations (Q_d = Q_s), c... | Critical EUEE Target Point |

### 4. Real-World Ethiopian Application & Technological Context
Agricultural staple crops like teff in Ethiopia exhibit price-inelastic demand, whereas non-essential imported luxury goods exhibit price-elastic demand.

### 5. EUEE Entrance Examination Strategy & Examiner Distractors
Very high frequency in EUEE: solving market equilibrium equations (Q_d = Q_s), calculating point/arc Price Elasticity of Demand, and finding consumer optimum (MRS_XY = P_X/P_Y).

### 6. Comprehensive Student Takeaway
Utility is maximized where MU_X/P_X = MU_Y/P_Y; market equilibrium occurs where Q_d = Q_s; |PED| dictates how price changes affect Total Revenue.

worked_examples.title: Worked Problem: Market Equilibrium & Price Elasticity of Demand
worked_examples.problem: The market for coffee in a regional town is given by the demand function Q_d = 120 - 4P and the supply function Q_s = 20 + 6P, where P is price in Birr and Q is quantity in kg. Find: (a) Equilibrium price and quantity, and (b) Point Price Elasticity of Demand at equilibrium.
worked_examples.step_solution:
1. Set Q_d = Q_s for equilibrium: 120 - 4P = 20 + 6P ⟹ 100 = 10P ⟹ P* = 10 Birr.
2. Substitute P* = 10 into Q_d: Q* = 120 - 4(10) = 80 kg.
3. Calculate Point PED: PED = (dQ_d / dP) × (P* / Q*) = (-4) × (10 / 80) = -40 / 80 = -0.5 (or |PED| = 0.5, Inelastic).
worked_examples.result: Equilibrium Price P* = 10 Birr, Equilibrium Quantity Q* = 80 kg, |PED| = 0.5 (Price Inelastic).
worked_examples.examiner_note: Since |PED| = 0.5 < 1, demand is inelastic at equilibrium, meaning a small price increase will raise total producer revenue.

practice_quiz.question: A consumer's Marginal Utility for Good X is 24 utils and for Good Y is 16 utils. If the price of Good X is 6 Birr, what must the price of Good Y be for the consumer to be in utility-maximizing equilibrium?

worked_example.title: Worked Problem: Market Equilibrium & Price Elasticity of Demand
worked_example.problem: The market for coffee in a regional town is given by the demand function Q_d = 120 - 4P and the supply function Q_s = 20 + 6P, where P is price in Birr and Q is quantity in kg. Find: (a) Equilibrium price and quantity, and (b) Point Price Elasticity of Demand at equilibrium.
worked_example.step_solution:
1. Set Q_d = Q_s for equilibrium: 120 - 4P = 20 + 6P ⟹ 100 = 10P ⟹ P* = 10 Birr.
2. Substitute P* = 10 into Q_d: Q* = 120 - 4(10) = 80 kg.
3. Calculate Point PED: PED = (dQ_d / dP) × (P* / Q*) = (-4) × (10 / 80) = -40 / 80 = -0.5 (or |PED| = 0.5, Inelastic).
worked_example.result: Equilibrium Price P* = 10 Birr, Equilibrium Quantity Q* = 80 kg, |PED| = 0.5 (Price Inelastic).
worked_example.examiner_note: Since |PED| = 0.5 < 1, demand is inelastic at equilibrium, meaning a small price increase will raise total producer revenue.

quiz_item.question: A consumer's Marginal Utility for Good X is 24 utils and for Good Y is 16 utils. If the price of Good X is 6 Birr, what must the price of Good Y be for the consumer to be in utility-maximizing equilibrium?
quiz_item.explanation: Consumer equilibrium requires MU_X / P_X = MU_Y / P_Y. Substituting values: 24 / 6 = 16 / P_Y ⟹ 4 = 16 / P_Y ⟹ P_Y = 16 / 4 = 4 Birr.

topics_covered.title: 2.1 Aggregate Demand (AD) Curve: Wealth, Interest Rate, and Exchange Rate Effects
topics_covered.topic_title: 2.1 Aggregate Demand (AD) Curve: Wealth, Interest Rate, and Exchange Rate Effects
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Downward slope of AD (Pigou real-balance effect, Keynes interest-rate effect, Mundell-Fleming net-export effect) and shifts.

• Scarcity, Opportunity Cost & PPF: Scarcity is the fundamental economic problem of unlimited wants versus limited resources. Opportunity Cost is the value of the single next-best alternative forgone. Production Possibility Frontier (PPF) illustrates scarcity (points outside are unattainable), efficiency (points on curve), inefficiency (points inside), and increasing opportunity cost (concave bowed-out shape).

• Consumer Behavior (Cardinal vs. Ordinal Utility): Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility: as more units of a good are consumed, Marginal Utility (MU = ΔTU / ΔQ) declines; Total Utility (TU) is maximized when MU = 0. Consumer Equilibrium (Cardinal): MU_X / P_X = MU_Y / P_Y. Ordinal Utility uses Indifference Curves (downward sloping, convex to origin, never intersect; slope = MRS_XY) tangent to the Budget Line (P_X·X + P_Y·Y = Income, slope = -P_X/P_Y).

• Law of Demand, Supply & Equilibrium: Demand (Q_d = a - bP) and Supply (Q_s = c + dP) intersect at Market Equilibrium (Q_d = Q_s). Price changes cause movement ALONG curves; non-price determinants (income, tastes, input costs, technology) SHIFT curves.

• Elasticities of Demand: Price Elasticity of Demand: PED = (%ΔQ_d) / (%ΔP) = (ΔQ / ΔP) × (P / Q). Elastic (|PED| > 1), Inelastic (|PED| < 1), Unitary (|PED| = 1). Cross-Price Elasticity (XED > 0 for substitutes, XED < 0 for complements). Income Elasticity (YED > 0 normal goods, YED < 0 inferior goods).
key_points: Consumer optimum occurs where the Marginal Rate of Substitution equals the price ratio: MRS_XY = MU_X / MU_Y = P_X / P_Y.
When demand is price INELASTIC (|PED| < 1), raising price INCREASES Total Revenue (TR = P × Q); when demand is ELASTIC (|PED| > 1), raising price DECREASES Total Revenue.
Two indifference curves can NEVER intersect because that would violate the transitivity and non-satiation axioms of consumer preference.

topics_covered.topic_title: 2.1 Aggregate Demand (AD) Curve: Wealth, Interest Rate, and Exchange Rate Effects
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Downward slope of AD (Pigou real-balance effect, Keynes interest-rate effect, Mundell-Fleming net-export effect) and shifts.

• Scarcity, Opportunity Cost & PPF: Scarcity is the fundamental economic problem of unlimited wants versus limited resources. Opportunity Cost is the value of the single next-best alternative forgone. Production Possibility Frontier (PPF) illustrates scarcity (points outside are unattainable), efficiency (points on curve), inefficiency (points inside), and increasing opportunity cost (concave bowed-out shape).

• Consumer Behavior (Cardinal vs. Ordinal Utility): Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility: as more units of a good are consumed, Marginal Utility (MU = ΔTU / ΔQ) declines; Total Utility (TU) is maximized when MU = 0. Consumer Equilibrium (Cardinal): MU_X / P_X = MU_Y / P_Y. Ordinal Utility uses Indifference Curves (downward sloping, convex to origin, never intersect; slope = MRS_XY) tangent to the Budget Line (P_X·X + P_Y·Y = Income, slope = -P_X/P_Y).

• Law of Demand, Supply & Equilibrium: Demand (Q_d = a - bP) and Supply (Q_s = c + dP) intersect at Market Equilibrium (Q_d = Q_s). Price changes cause movement ALONG curves; non-price determinants (income, tastes, input costs, technology) SHIFT curves.

• Elasticities of Demand: Price Elasticity of Demand: PED = (%ΔQ_d) / (%ΔP) = (ΔQ / ΔP) × (P / Q). Elastic (|PED| > 1), Inelastic (|PED| < 1), Unitary (|PED| = 1). Cross-Price Elasticity (XED > 0 for substitutes, XED < 0 for complements). Income Elasticity (YED > 0 normal goods, YED < 0 inferior goods).
key_points: Consumer optimum occurs where the Marginal Rate of Substitution equals the price ratio: MRS_XY = MU_X / MU_Y = P_X / P_Y.
When demand is price INELASTIC (|PED| < 1), raising price INCREASES Total Revenue (TR = P × Q); when demand is ELASTIC (|PED| > 1), raising price DECREASES Total Revenue.
Two indifference curves can NEVER intersect because that would violate the transitivity and non-satiation axioms of consumer preference.

worked_example.title: Worked Problem: Market Equilibrium & Price Elasticity of Demand
worked_example.problem: The market for coffee in a regional town is given by the demand function Q_d = 120 - 4P and the supply function Q_s = 20 + 6P, where P is price in Birr and Q is quantity in kg. Find: (a) Equilibrium price and quantity, and (b) Point Price Elasticity of Demand at equilibrium.
worked_example.step_solution:
1. Set Q_d = Q_s for equilibrium: 120 - 4P = 20 + 6P ⟹ 100 = 10P ⟹ P* = 10 Birr.
2. Substitute P* = 10 into Q_d: Q* = 120 - 4(10) = 80 kg.
3. Calculate Point PED: PED = (dQ_d / dP) × (P* / Q*) = (-4) × (10 / 80) = -40 / 80 = -0.5 (or |PED| = 0.5, Inelastic).
worked_example.result: Equilibrium Price P* = 10 Birr, Equilibrium Quantity Q* = 80 kg, |PED| = 0.5 (Price Inelastic).
worked_example.examiner_note: Since |PED| = 0.5 < 1, demand is inelastic at equilibrium, meaning a small price increase will raise total producer revenue.

topics_covered.topic_title: 2.2 Short-Run (SRAS) and Long-Run Aggregate Supply (LRAS) and Equilibrium
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Sticky-wage and misperception theories of SRAS, vertical LRAS at potential output Y*, recessionary vs inflationary gaps.

• Scarcity, Opportunity Cost & PPF: Scarcity is the fundamental economic problem of unlimited wants versus limited resources. Opportunity Cost is the value of the single next-best alternative forgone. Production Possibility Frontier (PPF) illustrates scarcity (points outside are unattainable), efficiency (points on curve), inefficiency (points inside), and increasing opportunity cost (concave bowed-out shape).

• Consumer Behavior (Cardinal vs. Ordinal Utility): Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility: as more units of a good are consumed, Marginal Utility (MU = ΔTU / ΔQ) declines; Total Utility (TU) is maximized when MU = 0. Consumer Equilibrium (Cardinal): MU_X / P_X = MU_Y / P_Y. Ordinal Utility uses Indifference Curves (downward sloping, convex to origin, never intersect; slope = MRS_XY) tangent to the Budget Line (P_X·X + P_Y·Y = Income, slope = -P_X/P_Y).

• Law of Demand, Supply & Equilibrium: Demand (Q_d = a - bP) and Supply (Q_s = c + dP) intersect at Market Equilibrium (Q_d = Q_s). Price changes cause movement ALONG curves; non-price determinants (income, tastes, input costs, technology) SHIFT curves.

• Elasticities of Demand: Price Elasticity of Demand: PED = (%ΔQ_d) / (%ΔP) = (ΔQ / ΔP) × (P / Q). Elastic (|PED| > 1), Inelastic (|PED| < 1), Unitary (|PED| = 1). Cross-Price Elasticity (XED > 0 for substitutes, XED < 0 for complements). Income Elasticity (YED > 0 normal goods, YED < 0 inferior goods).
key_points: Consumer optimum occurs where the Marginal Rate of Substitution equals the price ratio: MRS_XY = MU_X / MU_Y = P_X / P_Y.
When demand is price INELASTIC (|PED| < 1), raising price INCREASES Total Revenue (TR = P × Q); when demand is ELASTIC (|PED| > 1), raising price DECREASES Total Revenue.
Two indifference curves can NEVER intersect because that would violate the transitivity and non-satiation axioms of consumer preference.

worked_examples.title: Worked Problem: Market Equilibrium & Price Elasticity of Demand (2.1 Aggregate Demand (AD) Curve: Wealth, Interest Rate, and Exchange Rate Effects)
worked_examples.problem: The market for coffee in a regional town is given by the demand function Q_d = 120 - 4P and the supply function Q_s = 20 + 6P, where P is price in Birr and Q is quantity in kg. 1. Set Q_d = Q_s for equilibrium: 120 - 4P = 20 + 6P ⟹ 100 = 10P ⟹ P* = 10 Birr.

topics_covered.topic_title: 2.3 Classical, Keynesian, Monetarist, New Classical, and New Keynesian Schools
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Say’s Law vs Keynesian effective demand, Friedman’s Quantity Theory MV = PY, rational expectations, and policy debates.

• Scarcity, Opportunity Cost & PPF: Scarcity is the fundamental economic problem of unlimited wants versus limited resources. Opportunity Cost is the value of the single next-best alternative forgone. Production Possibility Frontier (PPF) illustrates scarcity (points outside are unattainable), efficiency (points on curve), inefficiency (points inside), and increasing opportunity cost (concave bowed-out shape).

• Consumer Behavior (Cardinal vs. Ordinal Utility): Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility: as more units of a good are consumed, Marginal Utility (MU = ΔTU / ΔQ) declines; Total Utility (TU) is maximized when MU = 0. Consumer Equilibrium (Cardinal): MU_X / P_X = MU_Y / P_Y. Ordinal Utility uses Indifference Curves (downward sloping, convex to origin, never intersect; slope = MRS_XY) tangent to the Budget Line (P_X·X + P_Y·Y = Income, slope = -P_X/P_Y).

• Law of Demand, Supply & Equilibrium: Demand (Q_d = a - bP) and Supply (Q_s = c + dP) intersect at Market Equilibrium (Q_d = Q_s). Price changes cause movement ALONG curves; non-price determinants (income, tastes, input costs, technology) SHIFT curves.

• Elasticities of Demand: Price Elasticity of Demand: PED = (%ΔQ_d) / (%ΔP) = (ΔQ / ΔP) × (P / Q). Elastic (|PED| > 1), Inelastic (|PED| < 1), Unitary (|PED| = 1). Cross-Price Elasticity (XED > 0 for substitutes, XED < 0 for complements). Income Elasticity (YED > 0 normal goods, YED < 0 inferior goods).
key_points: Consumer optimum occurs where the Marginal Rate of Substitution equals the price ratio: MRS_XY = MU_X / MU_Y = P_X / P_Y.
When demand is price INELASTIC (|PED| < 1), raising price INCREASES Total Revenue (TR = P × Q); when demand is ELASTIC (|PED| > 1), raising price DECREASES Total Revenue.
Two indifference curves can NEVER intersect because that would violate the transitivity and non-satiation axioms of consumer preference.

worked_examples.title: Worked Problem: Market Equilibrium & Price Elasticity of Demand
worked_examples.problem: The market for coffee in a regional town is given by the demand function Q_d = 120 - 4P and the supply function Q_s = 20 + 6P, where P is price in Birr and Q is quantity in kg. Find: (a) Equilibrium price and quantity, and (b) Point Price Elasticity of Demand at equilibrium.
worked_examples.step_solution:
1. Set Q_d = Q_s for equilibrium: 120 - 4P = 20 + 6P ⟹ 100 = 10P ⟹ P* = 10 Birr.
2. Substitute P* = 10 into Q_d: Q* = 120 - 4(10) = 80 kg.
3. Calculate Point PED: PED = (dQ_d / dP) × (P* / Q*) = (-4) × (10 / 80) = -40 / 80 = -0.5 (or |PED| = 0.5, Inelastic).
worked_examples.result: Equilibrium Price P* = 10 Birr, Equilibrium Quantity Q* = 80 kg, |PED| = 0.5 (Price Inelastic).
worked_examples.examiner_note: Since |PED| = 0.5 < 1, demand is inelastic at equilibrium, meaning a small price increase will raise total producer revenue.

Microeconomic demand and consumer theory explain how rational households allocate limited budgets across goods to maximize utility, and how market prices adjust to clear shortages and surpluses.

**Curriculum Syllabus Alignment:** Downward slope of AD (Pigou real-balance effect, Keynes interest-rate effect, Mundell-Fleming net-export effect) and shifts.

### 2. Systematic Concept Breakdown & Mechanisms
- **Consumer optimum occurs where the Marginal Rate of Substitution equals the price ratio**: Consumer optimum occurs where the Marginal Rate of Substitution equals the price ratio: MRS_XY = MU_X / MU_Y = P_X / P_Y.
- **Key Principle**: When demand is price INELASTIC (|PED| < 1), raising price INCREASES Total Revenue (TR = P × Q); when demand is ELASTIC (|PED| > 1), raising price DECREASES Total Revenue.
- **Key Principle**: Two indifference curves can NEVER intersect because that would violate the transitivity and non-satiation axioms of consumer preference.

worked_examples.title: Worked Problem: Market Equilibrium & Price Elasticity of Demand
worked_examples.problem: The market for coffee in a regional town is given by the demand function Q_d = 120 - 4P and the supply function Q_s = 20 + 6P, where P is price in Birr and Q is quantity in kg. Find: (a) Equilibrium price and quantity, and (b) Point Price Elasticity of Demand at equilibrium.
worked_examples.step_solution:
1. Set Q_d = Q_s for equilibrium: 120 - 4P = 20 + 6P ⟹ 100 = 10P ⟹ P* = 10 Birr.
2. Substitute P* = 10 into Q_d: Q* = 120 - 4(10) = 80 kg.
3. Calculate Point PED: PED = (dQ_d / dP) × (P* / Q*) = (-4) × (10 / 80) = -40 / 80 = -0.5 (or |PED| = 0.5, Inelastic).
worked_examples.result: Equilibrium Price P* = 10 Birr, Equilibrium Quantity Q* = 80 kg, |PED| = 0.5 (Price Inelastic).
worked_examples.examiner_note: Since |PED| = 0.5 < 1, demand is inelastic at equilibrium, meaning a small price increase will raise total producer revenue.

practice_quiz.question: A consumer's Marginal Utility for Good X is 24 utils and for Good Y is 16 utils. If the price of Good X is 6 Birr, what must the price of Good Y be for the consumer to be in utility-maximizing equilibrium?

Microeconomic demand and consumer theory explain how rational households allocate limited budgets across goods to maximize utility, and how market prices adjust to clear shortages and surpluses.

- **Key Principle**: Two indifference curves can NEVER intersect because that would violate the transitivity and non-satiation axioms of consumer preference.

worked_examples.title: Worked Problem: Market Equilibrium & Price Elasticity of Demand
worked_examples.problem: The market for coffee in a regional town is given by the demand function Q_d = 120 - 4P and the supply function Q_s = 20 + 6P, where P is price in Birr and Q is quantity in kg. Find: (a) Equilibrium price and quantity, and (b) Point Price Elasticity of Demand at equilibrium.
worked_examples.step_solution:
1. Set Q_d = Q_s for equilibrium: 120 - 4P = 20 + 6P ⟹ 100 = 10P ⟹ P* = 10 Birr.
2. Substitute P* = 10 into Q_d: Q* = 120 - 4(10) = 80 kg.
3. Calculate Point PED: PED = (dQ_d / dP) × (P* / Q*) = (-4) × (10 / 80) = -40 / 80 = -0.5 (or |PED| = 0.5, Inelastic).
worked_examples.result: Equilibrium Price P* = 10 Birr, Equilibrium Quantity Q* = 80 kg, |PED| = 0.5 (Price Inelastic).
worked_examples.examiner_note: Since |PED| = 0.5 < 1, demand is inelastic at equilibrium, meaning a small price increase will raise total producer revenue.

practice_quiz.question: A consumer's Marginal Utility for Good X is 24 utils and for Good Y is 16 utils. If the price of Good X is 6 Birr, what must the price of Good Y be for the consumer to be in utility-maximizing equilibrium?

worked_example.title: Worked Problem: Market Equilibrium & Price Elasticity of Demand
worked_example.problem: The market for coffee in a regional town is given by the demand function Q_d = 120 - 4P and the supply function Q_s = 20 + 6P, where P is price in Birr and Q is quantity in kg. Find: (a) Equilibrium price and quantity, and (b) Point Price Elasticity of Demand at equilibrium.
worked_example.step_solution:
1. Set Q_d = Q_s for equilibrium: 120 - 4P = 20 + 6P ⟹ 100 = 10P ⟹ P* = 10 Birr.
2. Substitute P* = 10 into Q_d: Q* = 120 - 4(10) = 80 kg.
3. Calculate Point PED: PED = (dQ_d / dP) × (P* / Q*) = (-4) × (10 / 80) = -40 / 80 = -0.5 (or |PED| = 0.5, Inelastic).
worked_example.result: Equilibrium Price P* = 10 Birr, Equilibrium Quantity Q* = 80 kg, |PED| = 0.5 (Price Inelastic).
worked_example.examiner_note: Since |PED| = 0.5 < 1, demand is inelastic at equilibrium, meaning a small price increase will raise total producer revenue.

quiz_item.question: A consumer's Marginal Utility for Good X is 24 utils and for Good Y is 16 utils. If the price of Good X is 6 Birr, what must the price of Good Y be for the consumer to be in utility-maximizing equilibrium?
quiz_item.explanation: Consumer equilibrium requires MU_X / P_X = MU_Y / P_Y. Substituting values: 24 / 6 = 16 / P_Y ⟹ 4 = 16 / P_Y ⟹ P_Y = 16 / 4 = 4 Birr.

topics_covered.title: 2.2 Short-Run (SRAS) and Long-Run Aggregate Supply (LRAS) and Equilibrium
topics_covered.topic_title: 2.2 Short-Run (SRAS) and Long-Run Aggregate Supply (LRAS) and Equilibrium
short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Sticky-wage and misperception theories of SRAS, vertical LRAS at potential output Y*, recessionary vs inflationary gaps.

• Scarcity, Opportunity Cost & PPF: Scarcity is the fundamental economic problem of unlimited wants versus limited resources. Opportunity Cost is the value of the single next-best alternative forgone. Production Possibility Frontier (PPF) illustrates scarcity (points outside are unattainable), efficiency (points on curve), inefficiency (points inside), and increasing opportunity cost (concave bowed-out shape).

• Consumer Behavior (Cardinal vs. Ordinal Utility): Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility: as more units of a good are consumed, Marginal Utility (MU = ΔTU / ΔQ) declines; Total Utility (TU) is maximized when MU = 0. Consumer Equilibrium (Cardinal): MU_X / P_X = MU_Y / P_Y. Ordinal Utility uses Indifference Curves (downward sloping, convex to origin, never intersect; slope = MRS_XY) tangent to the Budget Line (P_X·X + P_Y·Y = Income, slope = -P_X/P_Y).

• Law of Demand, Supply & Equilibrium: Demand (Q_d = a - bP) and Supply (Q_s = c + dP) intersect at Market Equilibrium (Q_d = Q_s). Price changes cause movement ALONG curves; non-price determinants (income, tastes, input costs, technology) SHIFT curves.

• Elasticities of Demand: Price Elasticity of Demand: PED = (%ΔQ_d) / (%ΔP) = (ΔQ / ΔP) × (P / Q). Elastic (|PED| > 1), Inelastic (|PED| < 1), Unitary (|PED| = 1). Cross-Price Elasticity (XED > 0 for substitutes, XED < 0 for complements). Income Elasticity (YED > 0 normal goods, YED < 0 inferior goods).
key_points: Consumer optimum occurs where the Marginal Rate of Substitution equals the price ratio: MRS_XY = MU_X / MU_Y = P_X / P_Y.
When demand is price INELASTIC (|PED| < 1), raising price INCREASES Total Revenue (TR = P × Q); when demand is ELASTIC (|PED| > 1), raising price DECREASES Total Revenue.
Two indifference curves can NEVER intersect because that would violate the transitivity and non-satiation axioms of consumer preference.

### 1. Theoretical Foundations & Governing Principles
Microeconomic demand and consumer theory explain how rational households allocate limited budgets across goods to maximize utility, and how market prices adjust to clear shortages and surpluses.

**Curriculum Syllabus Alignment:** Sticky-wage and misperception theories of SRAS, vertical LRAS at potential output Y*, recessionary vs inflationary gaps.

### 2. Systematic Concept Breakdown & Mechanisms
- **Consumer optimum occurs where the Marginal Rate of Substitution equals the price ratio**: Consumer optimum occurs where the Marginal Rate of Substitution equals the price ratio: MRS_XY = MU_X / MU_Y = P_X / P_Y.
- **Key Principle**: When demand is price INELASTIC (|PED| < 1), raising price INCREASES Total Revenue (TR = P × Q); when demand is ELASTIC (|PED| > 1), raising price DECREASES Total Revenue.
- **Key Principle**: Two indifference curves can NEVER intersect because that would violate the transitivity and non-satiation axioms of consumer preference.

### 3. Core Reference Table & Visual Schema
**Visual / Experimental Schema:**
```text
Consumer Optimum & Equilibrium: [Indifference Curve Tangent to Budget Line: MRS_XY = P_X/P_Y] ──> [Individual Demand] ──> [Market Equilibrium: Q_d = Q_s].
```

| **Examination Traps** | Very high frequency in EUEE: solving market equilibrium equations (Q_d = Q_s), c... | Critical EUEE Target Point |

### 4. Real-World Ethiopian Application & Technological Context
Agricultural staple crops like teff in Ethiopia exhibit price-inelastic demand, whereas non-essential imported luxury goods exhibit price-elastic demand.

### 5. EUEE Entrance Examination Strategy & Examiner Distractors
Very high frequency in EUEE: solving market equilibrium equations (Q_d = Q_s), calculating point/arc Price Elasticity of Demand, and finding consumer optimum (MRS_XY = P_X/P_Y).

### 6. Comprehensive Student Takeaway
Utility is maximized where MU_X/P_X = MU_Y/P_Y; market equilibrium occurs where Q_d = Q_s; |PED| dictates how price changes affect Total Revenue.

short_notes: • Curriculum Focus: Sticky-wage and misperception theories of SRAS, vertical LRAS at potential output Y*, recessionary vs inflationary gaps.

• Scarcity, Opportunity Cost & PPF: Scarcity is the fundamental economic problem of unlimited wants versus limited resources. Opportunity Cost is the value of the single next-best alternative forgone. Production Possibility Frontier (PPF) illustrates scarcity (points outside are unattainable), efficiency (points on curve), inefficiency (points inside), and increasing opportunity cost (concave bowed-out shape).

• Consumer Behavior (Cardinal vs. Ordinal Utility): Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility: as more units of a good are consumed, Marginal Utility (MU = ΔTU / ΔQ) declines; Total Utility (TU) is maximized when MU = 0. Consumer Equilibrium (Cardinal): MU_X / P_X = MU_Y / P_Y. Ordinal Utility uses Indifference Curves (downward sloping, convex to origin, never intersect; slope = MRS_XY) tangent to the Budget Line (P_X·X + P_Y·Y = Income, slope = -P_X/P_Y).

• Law of Demand, Supply & Equilibrium: Demand (Q_d = a - bP) and Supply (Q_s = c + dP) intersect at Market Equilibrium (Q_d = Q_s). Price changes cause movement ALONG curves; non-price determinants (income, tastes, input costs, technology) SHIFT curves.

• Elasticities of Demand: Price Elasticity of Demand: PED = (%ΔQ_d) / (%ΔP) = (ΔQ / ΔP) × (P / Q). Elastic (|PED| > 1), Inelastic (|PED| < 1), Unitary (|PED| = 1). Cross-Price Elasticity (XED > 0 for substitutes, XED < 0 for complements). Income Elasticity (YED > 0 normal goods, YED < 0 inferior goods).
key_points: Consumer optimum occurs where the Marginal Rate of Substitution equals the price ratio: MRS_XY = MU_X / MU_Y = P_X / P_Y.
When demand is price INELASTIC (|PED| < 1), raising price INCREASES Total Revenue (TR = P × Q); when demand is ELASTIC (|PED| > 1), raising price DECREASES Total Revenue.
Two indifference curves can NEVER intersect because that would violate the transitivity and non-satiation axioms of consumer preference.

worked_examples.title: Worked Problem: Market Equilibrium & Price Elasticity of Demand
worked_examples.problem: The market for coffee in a regional town is given by the demand function Q_d = 120 - 4P and the supply function Q_s = 20 + 6P, where P is price in Birr and Q is quantity in kg. Find: (a) Equilibrium price and quantity, and (b) Point Price Elasticity of Demand at equilibrium.
worked_examples.step_solution:
1. Set Q_d = Q_s for equilibrium: 120 - 4P = 20 + 6P ⟹ 100 = 10P ⟹ P* = 10 Birr.
2. Substitute P* = 10 into Q_d: Q* = 120 - 4(10) = 80 kg.
3. Calculate Point PED: PED = (dQ_d / dP) × (P* / Q*) = (-4) × (10 / 80) = -40 / 80 = -0.5 (or |PED| = 0.5, Inelastic).
worked_examples.result: Equilibrium Price P* = 10 Birr, Equilibrium Quantity Q* = 80 kg, |PED| = 0.5 (Price Inelastic).
worked_examples.examiner_note: Since |PED| = 0.5 < 1, demand is inelastic at equilibrium, meaning a small price increase will raise total producer revenue.

practice_quiz.question: A consumer's Marginal Utility for Good X is 24 utils and for Good Y is 16 utils. If the price of Good X is 6 Birr, what must the price of Good Y be for the consumer to be in utility-maximizing equilibrium?
practice_quiz.explanation: Consumer equilibrium requires MU_X / P_X = MU_Y / P_Y. Substituting values: 24 / 6 = 16 / P_Y ⟹ 4 = 16 / P_Y ⟹ P_Y = 16 / 4 = 4 Birr.

core_formulas_rules.explanation: Consumer Behavior (Cardinal vs. Ordinal Utility): Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility: as more units of a good are consumed, Marginal Utility (MU = ΔTU / ΔQ) declines; Total Utility (TU) is maximized when MU = 0. Consumer Equilibrium (Cardinal): MU_X / P_X = MU_Y / P_Y. Ordinal Utility uses Indifference Curves (downward sloping, convex to origin, never intersect; slope = MRS_XY) tangent to the Budget Line (P_X·X + P_Y·Y = Income, slope = -P_X/P_Y).
core_formulas_rules.units_conditions: Standard Ethiopian curriculum specifications and SI units apply.

core_formulas_rules.explanation: Law of Demand, Supply & Equilibrium: Demand (Q_d = a - bP) and Supply (Q_s = c + dP) intersect at Market Equilibrium (Q_d = Q_s). Price changes cause movement ALONG curves; non-price determinants (income, tastes, input costs, technology) SHIFT curves.

worked_examples.title: Worked Problem: Market Equilibrium & Price Elasticity of Demand
worked_examples.problem: The market for coffee in a regional town is given by the demand function Q_d = 120 - 4P and the supply function Q_s = 20 + 6P, where P is price in Birr and Q is quantity in kg. Find: (a) Equilibrium price and quantity, and (b) Point Price Elasticity of Demand at equilibrium.
worked_examples.step_solution:
1. Set Q_d = Q_s for equilibrium: 120 - 4P = 20 + 6P ⟹ 100 = 10P ⟹ P* = 10 Birr.
2. Substitute P* = 10 into Q_d: Q* = 120 - 4(10) = 80 kg.
3. Calculate Point PED: PED = (dQ_d / dP) × (P* / Q*) = (-4) × (10 / 80) = -40 / 80 = -0.5 (or |PED| = 0.5, Inelastic).
worked_examples.result: Equilibrium Price P* = 10 Birr, Equilibrium Quantity Q* = 80 kg, |PED| = 0.5 (Price Inelastic).
worked_examples.examiner_note: Since |PED| = 0.5 < 1, demand is inelastic at equilibrium, meaning a small price increase will raise total producer revenue.

practice_quiz.question: A consumer's Marginal Utility for Good X is 24 utils and for Good Y is 16 utils. If the price of Good X is 6 Birr, what must the price of Good Y be for the consumer to be in utility-maximizing equilibrium?
practice_quiz.explanation: Consumer equilibrium requires MU_X / P_X = MU_Y / P_Y. Substituting values: 24 / 6 = 16 / P_Y ⟹ 4 = 16 / P_Y ⟹ P_Y = 16 / 4 = 4 Birr.
